paper_context.research_question: How can one semi-automatically create data-to-text corpora from existing knowledge bases that better support learning of wide-coverage micro-planners, and how do such corpora compare (linguistically and computationally) to existing crowdsourced benchmarks?
main_claims: A semi-automatic framework combining ILP-based content selection from KBs (DBpedia) with selective crowdsourcing can produce data-to-text corpora (DBPNLG) suitable for training micro-planners.

DBPNLG, though smaller than the RNNLG dataset, is more diverse in input attributes, input patterns and input shapes (including deeper tree structures) and produces lexically and syntactically richer texts.

The greater diversity and complexity of DBPNLG make generation harder for standard sequence-to-sequence models (higher perplexity and lower BLEU), indicating it is a more challenging benchmark for learning micro-planning operations.
The dataset creation procedure yields a good semantic match between data and text (via crowd validation), hence focusing evaluation on micro-planning rather than content selection.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Dataset coverage and diversity: number of attributes, input patterns, input shapes (depth), and ratio of inputs to input-patterns.
Textual complexity: tokens per text, sentences per text, lexical diversity (CTTR), lexical sophistication (LS), vocabulary size and paraphrase multiplicity (texts per input).
Semantic fidelity: proportion of data-text pairs passing crowd validation (semantic adequacy), and manual spot checks.
Learning difficulty: performance of baseline generation models (seq2seq) measured by perplexity and BLEU under controlled delexicalisation settings.
Reproducibility and applicability: clarity and generality of the content-selection procedure (ILP and bigram models) to other RDF KBs and scalability of crowdsourcing/validation steps.
Quality control of crowdsourcing: description and effectiveness of anti-spam validators, manual filtering rates, and corpus loss percentage.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a semi-automatic pipeline (ILP-based content selection from DBpedia category graphs + selective crowdsourcing with validation) to create DBPNLG, a resource aimed at training micro-planners. The core argument chain: 1) existing crowdsourced datasets (e.g., RNNLG) are larger but limited in input shape depth and lexical/syntactic diversity; 2) a content selection procedure using sibling/chain bigram models and ILP yields varied input shapes and patterns (including deeper trees); 3) selective crowdsourcing with clarifications and multi-step verification yields high semantic fidelity; 4) DBPNLG therefore supports learning of micro-planning operations and is empirically more diverse though smaller; 5) standard seq2seq baselines perform worse on DBPNLG, indicating greater learning challenge. Overall the reasoning is coherent and the empirical analyses align with the claims, but several inference steps rely on assumptions or limited experimental choices (single seq2seq architecture, balanced 13K sampling, limited reporting of validation/inter-annotator metrics, partial ILP details). Key strengths are the explicit pipeline, multi-metric dataset comparison, and using crowdsourced single-triple verbalizations to bootstrap multi-triple texts. Main weaknesses are gaps in methodological transparency (ILP/objective/solver; validator/agreement stats), limited robustness checks for the neural comparisons, and claims of generalisability with limited empirical evidence beyond six DBpedia categories.
logical_argument_graph: Node L0: Motivation — Need corpora to train wide-coverage micro-planners (Intro, Section 2).

Node L1: Shortcomings of prior approaches — domain-specific datasets are narrow; expert-annotated corpora costly and surface-focused; crowdsourced benchmarks use artificial, depth-1 inputs (Section 2).
Edge L1->L0: motivates the proposed approach to address coverage and micro-planning needs.
Node L2: Proposed framework — content selection (ILP + three bigram models) + selective crowdsourcing + verification (Section 3).
Edge L2->L1: framework intended to remedy prior shortcomings (uses KB data; produces deeper input shapes; crowd authors text from data).

Node L3: Implementation on DBpedia — select 6 categories, extract category graphs, learn S/C/M bigram models, ILP selects subtrees size 1–7; crowdsourcing collects/verifies verbalisations (Section 3.2–3.3).
Edge L3->L2: concrete instantiation demonstrating pipeline feasibility.
Node L4: Empirical dataset comparisons — DBPNLG has more attributes, more input shapes (58 vs 6), lower inputs-per-pattern ratio, higher lexical diversity and multi-sentence texts (Section 4.1–4.2).
Edge L4->L3: results of the DBpedia instantiation claimed to support framework's goals (diversity, depth).
Node L5: Learning difficulty evidence — seq2seq baseline shows higher perplexity & lower BLEU on DBPNLG (13K balanced sampling), indicating greater challenge (Section 4.3).
Edge L5->L4: connects dataset structural properties to learning difficulty.

Node L6: Semantic fidelity claim — crowdsourced verification (5 votes, 3 negative => reject) produced 8.7% corpus loss; thus dataset focuses on micro-planning not content selection errors (Section 3.3).
Edge L6->L3: supports the claim that data-text pairs are semantically matched.
Node L7: Generalisability claim — method applicable to other RDF KBs (Conclusion, Section 3).
Edge L7->L2: asserts broader applicability though empirical support limited to selected categories.

Critical weak links identified in graph: (a) L5 relies on one model, one training size, and possibly preprocessing choices (delex modes) — threatens generality of learning-difficulty inference; (b) L6 lacks inter-annotator agreement and error-type breakdown — weakens confidence the verification removes systematic content mismatches; (c) L3->L4: ILP/bigram modelling details (objective, constraints, solver) insufficiently specified — raises risk of undocumented selection bias affecting diversity claims; (d) L7 is asserted but only weakly evidenced (six categories only).

strengths.title: Clear, reproducible high-level pipeline
strengths.description: The paper presents a concrete, modular pipeline (content selection via bigram models + ILP; single-triple verbalisations; merging; verification) that can be implemented by other researchers.
evidence: Section 3 provides stepwise description of selecting category graphs, learning sibling/chain/interpolated bigram models (SRILM), ILP subtree selection and the four-step crowdsourcing protocol.

strengths.title: Comprehensive multi-dimensional dataset analysis
strengths.description: Authors evaluate DBPNLG vs RNNLG across many interpretable metrics (attributes, input patterns, shapes, tokens/sentences, CTTR, LS, texts-per-input) linking structural properties to linguistic variety.

strengths.title: Thoughtful crowdsourcing design to reduce semantic mismatch
strengths.description: The crowdsourcing workflow (clarifying properties, collecting single-triple verbalizations, merging, multi-annotator verification) is designed to minimize semantic drift between data and text.

concerns.title: Insufficient ILP and bigram model implementation details
concerns.description: The ILP selection objective, constraints, solver choice/settings and how the three bigram models are combined (if at all) are not fully specified; without these details the content selection step is not reproducible and may introduce undocumented biases.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes the high-level approach (S/C/M models, ILP selecting subtrees size 1–7) but omits objective function, constraints, solver name, and candidate generation procedures.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add the ILP mathematical formulation (objective, variables, constraints), specify solver and parameters, provide examples of alternate solutions and an ablation that shows differences between using S-Model, C-Model, M-Model and a random baseline.

concerns.title: Neural baseline limited to one architecture, one training size, no statistical analysis
concerns.description: Using a single off-the-shelf seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow tutorial) trained on a balanced 13K sample limits the generality of claims about dataset difficulty; no hyperparameter search, variance estimates, or significance tests are reported.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run additional architectures (Wen et al.'s model, tuned LSTM/transformer variants), vary training sizes (full dataset vs 13K), report standard deviations across runs, and include statistical significance tests comparing perplexity/BLEU.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing verification lacks inter-annotator/agreement and error-type analysis
concerns.description: Reporting only an aggregate 8.7% corpus loss leaves unclear the types and rates of residual semantic mismatches; no inter-annotator agreement measures or per-category verification statistics are given.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes verification (5 votes, reject if 3 negatives) but does not report Kappa, per-criterion agreement, or examples of rejected vs accepted errors.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide inter-annotator agreement statistics per criterion, per-category breakdown of rejection rates, and a sampled confusion analysis of remaining errors to demonstrate residual semantic fidelity.

concerns.title: Generalisability claim under-supported empirically
concerns.description: The paper claims applicability to other RDF KBs, but only detailed results for six DBpedia categories are shown; manual clarifications per category may not scale and could affect reproducibility.
evidence: Section 3 states applicability to other KBs but empirical evidence limited to six categories; authors mention additional 14 categories were collected but not reported.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either include experiments or summary statistics from additional categories/KBs, or quantify human effort needed for property clarification and its variance across categories.

evidence: Section 4.3 describes two delexicalisation modes implemented via exact token matches; no ablation or error analysis of delex steps is given.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe tokenization/normalization rules, report how many entities failed exact matches, and rerun model comparisons with a robust delex pipeline (entity spans via linking or canonicalization) to confirm results.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include targeted probes or tasks (e.g., controlled aggregation transformations, referring expression tests) and show model performance on these to substantiate claims about micro-planning suitability.

alternative_interpretations: Model difficulty (higher perplexity / lower BLEU) may be driven more by larger vocabulary and sparser pattern instantiation (low inputs-per-pattern) than by structural depth per se; better tuned or architecture-adapted models might close the gap.

The higher diversity measured could partly stem from the content-selection objective (optimising bigram co-occurrence) which may favour rare or idiosyncratic property combinations; some of the measured 'diversity' might reduce learnability if it includes noisy or unnatural pairings.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a semi-automatic pipeline to build data-to-text corpora (DBPNLG) from DBpedia: (1) extract category graphs; (2) learn property bigram models (sibling, chain, interpolated) with SRILM; (3) formulate an ILP to select subtrees of size 1–7 maximizing bigram probability to create inputs of varied shapes and depths; (4) collect verbalizations via a 4-step CrowdFlower pipeline (clarify properties, collect single-triple sentences, merge for multi-triple inputs, and verify with five validators). The resulting DBPNLG is compared to the RNNLG dataset (Wen et al. 2016) on data diversity (attributes, input-patterns, shapes), textual complexity (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), semantic fidelity (verification loss 8.7%), and learnability (3-layer seq2seq with attention trained on balanced 13K samples; DBPNLG shows higher perplexity and lower BLEU). The paper argues DBPNLG is more diverse and more challenging for current seq2seq models and suitable for training and evaluating micro-planning components. Key methodological choices: bigram co-occurrence as coherence proxy, ILP optimization for subtree selection, crowdsourced single-triple verbalizations as building blocks for multi-triple texts, and majority-vote verification. Evidence is provided in descriptive statistics and baseline neural experiments, but full numeric detail, statistical testing, ILP formulation specifics, and annotation reliability metrics are missing or underreported. The claims about generalisability to other RDF KBs and about the dataset focusing learning on micro-planning are plausible but not fully validated by targeted experiments or multi-KB reproduction.
logical_argument_graph: Goal: create corpora to train wide-coverage micro-planners
-> Need: data units that (i) reflect KB structure, (ii) vary in shape/size to induce syntactic variety, (iii) have accurate human text aligned
-> Method: extract category graphs from DBpedia (up to 500 entities) to obtain property co-occurrence statistics
-> Model choice: train SRILM bigram models (sibling, chain, interpolated) to proxy coherence
-> Selection: formulate ILP to select subtrees (1-7 triples) maximizing bigram probability => produces varied shapes
-> Crowdsourcing: clarify property labels; crowdwrite single-triple verbalizations; instruct merging to create multi-triple texts; verify with 5 annotators and majority rule => final DBPNLG
-> Evaluation data analysis: compute attributes, input-patterns, shapes, tokens/sentences, CTTR, LS, texts-per-input
-> Learning difficulty test: train standard seq2seq (3-layer, 512 units) on balanced 13K samples and compute perplexity/BLEU under delexicalisation modes
-> Conclusion: DBPNLG is more diverse, semantically validated, and more challenging for seq2seq models, thus useful for micro-planning research

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that a semi-automatic pipeline — (i) extracting category graphs from DBpedia; (ii) learning sibling/chain/interpolated bigram models of properties; (iii) formulating selection of coherent subtrees (1–7 RDF triples) as an ILP; and (iv) using a staged crowdsourcing process (single-triple verbalizations, merging, validators, majority-vote verification) — yields a data-to-text corpus (DBPNLG) that is better suited to training and evaluating micro-planning components than existing crowdsourced benchmarks (notably Wen et al. 2016's RNNLG). The reasoning chain is: KB-driven content selection produces varied input shapes (including deeper trees) → varied shapes map to richer syntactic phenomena in texts → crowd-authored and verified texts maintain semantic fidelity → richer data/text diversity increases learning difficulty for vanilla seq2seq models (measured by perplexity/BLEU), therefore the resource better exercises micro-planning subtasks. The manuscript supports these steps with dataset statistics (attributes, shapes, input-pattern ratios, lexical metrics), a description of the ILP+bigram procedure, crowdsourcing loss rate (~8.7%), and a proof-of-concept seq2seq comparison on balanced 13K samples per dataset. The contribution is positioned as an incremental but targeted innovation: combining prior ideas (KB-derived inputs, statistical co-occurrence for coherence, ILP selection, crowdsourced verbalisation) into a pipeline explicitly tuned to produce inputs that induce micro-planning phenomena and provide a challenging resource.
logical_argument_graph: P1: KBs (DBpedia) contain many categorized entities and structured triples → can provide realistic input fragments for NLG.
P2: Existing crowdsourced datasets (e.g., RNNLG) enumerate shallow attribute combinations (depth=1) → limited input shapes and syntactic variety.
P3: Learning micro-planning requires varied input shapes/sizes to surface diverse syntactic constructions (aggregation, relative clauses, segmentation, referring expressions).
P4: Bigram co-occurrence (sibling/chain) learned from category graphs can approximate property coherence; ILP can pick coherent subgraphs of varied sizes.
P5: Crowdsourced single-triple verbalizations combined and verified by majority vote yield semantically faithful texts paired with those subgraphs.
C1: The above pipeline yields DBPNLG, a KB-grounded, linguistically richer dataset than RNNLG by several metrics (attributes, shapes, lexical measures).
P6: Richer/less repetitive datasets are harder for standard seq2seq models → higher perplexity/lower BLEU in experiments.
C2: DBPNLG is a more challenging benchmark for learning micro-planning operations and better suited for training KB verbalisers than RNNLG.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a semi-automatic pipeline to create KB-grounded data-to-text corpora targeted at micro-planning. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a semi-automatic pipeline to build a KB-grounded data-to-text corpus (DBPNLG) intended to better exercise NLG micro-planning subtasks. The pipeline: (1) extract category graphs from DBpedia, (2) learn property bigram models (sibling/chain/interpolated) using SRILM, (3) formulate content selection as an ILP to pick subtrees of 1–7 triples producing varied input shapes, and (4) run a four-step CrowdFlower pipeline to collect/verifiy single-triple verbalisations and merged multi-triple texts (three verbalisations per input, five validators per verbalisation; 8.7% corpus loss). Empirical comparisons versus the RNNLG dataset are performed across data statistics (attributes, input patterns, shapes), textual metrics (tokens, sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication, texts-per-input), and a baseline neural evaluation (3-layer 512-unit seq2seq with attention trained on balanced 13K samples per dataset under two delexicalisation modes). The manuscript's reconstructed argument: ILP+bigram selection yields deeper/more varied input shapes → those shapes elicit richer syntactic/lexical phenomena in texts (confirmed by textual metrics) → crowdsourced verification achieves adequate semantic fidelity (8.7% removal) → seq2seq baselines perform worse on DBPNLG, implying greater learning difficulty and better exercising of micro-planning tasks. Evidence in the paper supports most components (pipeline description, dataset statistics, crowdsourcing protocol, baseline experiments), but several inference steps are only partially supported due to missing methodological details (ILP formulation and solver settings), limited reliability statistics for crowd validation (inter-annotator agreement, error breakdown), reliance on a single neural baseline / fixed training size, and lack of targeted evaluations testing whether models actually learn specific micro-planning operations (e.g., aggregation, referring expression generation). I flag these as uncertainties and provide concrete suggestions and alternative interpretations below.

P2: Extracting category graphs and learning sibling/chain bigram co-occurrence models captures topical/discourse coherence among DBpedia properties.
P3: Formulating subtree selection as ILP maximizing bigram probability yields input units with varied shape/depth (1–7 triples) and diverse attribute combinations.
P4: Crowdsourced single-triple verbalizations plus merging and majority-vote verification yields semantically faithful and linguistically varied texts.
C1: The resulting DBPNLG corpus exhibits higher attribute counts, more input patterns, more input shapes (including deeper trees), longer/more complex texts, and greater lexical diversity than RNNLG.
P5: Seq2seq baselines trained on balanced 13K samples show higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG than on RNNLG.
C2: DBPNLG is a more challenging benchmark for learning micro-planning operations and is suitable for training KB verbalisers.

identified_claims.claim_text: A semi-automatic framework combining ILP-based content selection from knowledge bases (DBpedia) with selective crowdsourcing can produce data-to-text corpora (DBPNLG) suitable for training micro-planners.
evidence: Detailed pipeline description in Section 3 including ILP-based selection and a four-step crowdsourcing procedure
Example inputs and resulting text (Example 1) illustrating micro-planning phenomena (lexicalisation, aggregation, sentence segmentation)
Dataset uploaded with submission (authors state DBPNLG is available)
uncertainty_flags: The link from dataset properties to improved micro-planner learning is indirect: only baseline seq2seq difficulty is shown, not targeted evaluations of micro-planning subtasks.
Generality of suitability across domains/KBs is asserted but empirical evidence is limited to six DBpedia categories in this paper.

identified_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG is more diverse than RNNLG
identified_claims.claim_text: DBPNLG, though smaller than the RNNLG dataset, is more diverse in input attributes, input patterns and input shapes (including deeper tree structures) and produces lexically and syntactically richer texts.
evidence: Reported counts: 172 attributes (DBPNLG) vs 108 (RNNLG); 58 distinct shapes vs 6 in RNNLG; 49.6% of DBPNLG inputs have depth >1
Textual metrics: higher tokens per text, sentences per text, higher CTTR and higher lexical sophistication reported in Section 4.2
uncertainty_flags: Not all numeric tables reproduced in the excerpt; confirm whether these metrics are computed over full datasets or sampled subsets.
Some metrics (e.g., vocabulary sizes) are sensitive to preprocessing/tokenization choices—details not fully specified.

identified_claims.claim_text: The greater diversity and complexity of DBPNLG make generation harder for standard sequence-to-sequence models (higher perplexity and lower BLEU), indicating it is a more challenging benchmark for learning micro-planning operations.
evidence: Seq2seq (3-layer, 512 units, attention) trained on balanced 13K samples shows higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG across both delexicalisation modes
Authors report Table 5 (perplexity/BLEU) supporting this
uncertainty_flags: Only one seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow tutorial) and single training size used—results may not generalize to other architectures or larger data.
No statistical testing or variance reporting; hyperparameter tuning and training stability details are lacking.

identified_claims.claim_text: The dataset creation procedure yields a good semantic match between data and text via crowd validation (fluency/semantic adequacy/grammaticality checks and majority vote), hence focusing evaluation on micro-planning rather than content selection.
evidence: Four-step crowdsourcing: property clarification, single-triple verbalizations, merging, and verification with five annotators per verbalisation
Reported corpus loss after verification: 8.7%
uncertainty_flags: No inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa) or per-category error breakdown reported; 8.7% aggregate loss is informative but coarse.
Manual checks and worker banning are described but criteria and scale (how many banned, how many post-hoc removals) are not given.

identified_claims.claim_label: Framework generalisable to other RDF KBs
identified_claims.claim_text: The method can be used to create a data-to-text corpus from any knowledge base where entities are categorised and many entities belong to the same category (e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData).
evidence: Explicit statement in Section 3 that the method applies to KBs with categorical entities and many instances
Examples of other KBs listed in Section 3 and Conclusion
uncertainty_flags: Only empirical application to six DBpedia categories is shown; no experimental reproduction on other KBs or large-scale cost/effort analysis for property clarifications.
Scalability concerns: manual clarification per category may be non-trivial for heterogeneous KBs.

identified_claims.claim_label: Content selection uses ILP + bigram models
identified_claims.claim_text: Content selection is done by extracting category graphs, learning three types of DBpedia property bigram models (sibling, chained, interpolated) and formulating selection as an ILP to select subtrees (1–7 triples) with maximal bigram probability.
evidence: Procedure described: category graphs (up to 500 entity graphs), S-Model/C-Model/M-Model via SRILM, ILP selecting subtrees maximizing bigram probability with size constraints
uncertainty_flags: ILP objective function, constraints, solver choice, runtime and potential regularisation/coverage constraints are not specified.
Sensitivity of selected shapes to bigram model smoothing, category sample size, and interpolation weights is not reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Because DBPNLG pairs data units of varying sizes and shapes with texts ranging from single clauses to multi-sentence texts, it is appropriate for exercising micro-planning subtasks such as lexicalisation, aggregation, sentence segmentation and referring expression generation.
evidence: Examples showing aggregation and multi-sentence realizations (Example 1 and 6)
Reported longer texts, more sentences per text, and higher texts-per-input supporting paraphrase learning
uncertainty_flags: No controlled evaluations demonstrate that models trained on DBPNLG learn specific micro-planning operations better than on other datasets.
Presence of phenomena does not guarantee learnability without targeted supervision or architectures.

strengths.title: Clear, coherent pipeline combining automatic selection and crowdsourcing
strengths.description: The paper provides a logically consistent pipeline linking content selection from DBpedia with staged crowdsourcing and validation to construct a KB-grounded corpus.
evidence: Section 3 describes extracting category graphs, learning bigram models, ILP selection, and a four-step CrowdFlower workflow
Worked examples (e.g., Example 1) illustrating how content selection maps to text collection

strengths.title: Multi-dimensional empirical comparison versus an established benchmark
strengths.description: DBPNLG is compared to RNNLG across data structure (attributes, patterns, shapes), textual metrics (tokens, sentences, CTTR, LS), and baseline model performance (perplexity/BLEU).
evidence: Sections 4.1 and 4.2 present attribute counts, shapes, input-pattern ratios, CTTR and LS comparisons
Section 4.3 reports seq2seq baseline comparisons under two delexicalisation modes

strengths.title: Thoughtful crowdsourcing design to reduce semantic mismatch
strengths.description: The collection pipeline uses property clarifications, single-triple verbalisations used as building blocks, automated validators and five-way verification to increase data-text fidelity.
evidence: Section 3.3 details 12 JS validators, manual checks, banning, and the 4-step process culminating in five answers per verbalisation
Reported overall corpus loss of 8.7% after verification

concerns.title: Insufficient ILP specification and reproducibility details
concerns.description: The ILP objective, constraints, solver used, runtime, and sensitivity analyses (to bigram smoothing/interpolation weights and sample sizes) are not described, threatening reproducibility and raising the possibility of selection bias in input shapes.
evidence: Section 3.2 says 'formulated as an ILP to select subtrees of Ge with maximal bigram probability' but gives no formal objective or constraints
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flagged missing ILP formulation and solver settings
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include the ILP mathematical formulation, list constraints and variables, specify solver and parameters, report runtimes and provide ablation/sensitivity tests (e.g., varying interpolation weight, sample size, constraint on shape diversity). Release code and sample ILP instances.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing verification lacks reliability and audit statistics
concerns.description: Verification is described (five annotators, majority rule) and an aggregate 8.7% loss is reported, but no inter-annotator agreement, per-category removal rates, error-type breakdown, or worker qualification statistics are provided—limiting confidence in semantic fidelity claims.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes verification protocol but does not report kappa, proportion of disagreements, or examples of remaining errors
Shared analysis notes absence of inter-annotator agreement and detailed post-hoc validation logs
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement (pairwise/ Fleiss/Kappa), per-category verification outcomes, representative examples of removed/retained borderline cases, worker qualification metrics, and provide anonymized validator logs for audit.

concerns.title: Neural baseline evaluation too narrow to support general claims
concerns.description: Model-difficulty claims rest on a single seq2seq implementation trained on a single balanced sample size (13K), without hyperparameter tuning, variance reporting, or alternative architectures—raising doubts about generality.
evidence: Section 4.3 uses the TensorFlow translation tutorial code (Vinyals et al., 2015) with 3 layers and 512 units; authors note alternative optimized implementations exist but were not used
Shared analysis and prior reviewers highlight reliance on one architecture and training size
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand experiments: evaluate multiple architectures (e.g., optimized implementations from Wen et al., copy/slot- aware models), vary training set sizes including full datasets, perform hyperparameter search, report variance across random seeds, and run statistical tests to quantify significance of performance differences.

concerns.title: Gap between presence of phenomena and evidence models learn micro-planning
concerns.description: The paper shows DBPNLG contains phenomena (aggregation, referring expressions, sentence segmentation) but does not present targeted evaluations (diagnostic tests) showing models trained on DBPNLG learn or improve on these specific micro-planning operations.
evidence: Examples and corpus statistics document presence of micro-planning phenomena, but no controlled probing tasks are provided
Shared analysis recommends targeted tests for aggregation/referring generation
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide targeted evaluation experiments: controlled test suites for aggregation, referring expression generation, and sentence splitting/merging; measure model behavior on these probes and compare to RNNLG-trained models.

concerns.title: Generalisability claim to other KBs is under-evidenced
concerns.description: Authors assert the pipeline generalises to other RDF KBs, but only show six DBpedia categories; manual property clarification is said to be required and could be a scaling bottleneck.
evidence: Section 3 and Conclusion state applicability to MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData, but no experiments beyond DBpedia categories are presented
Shared analysis notes additional 14 categories were gathered for content but texts not yet collected
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either demonstrate pipeline application to at least one non-DBpedia KB or provide a detailed costing (human effort per category) of property clarification and crowdsourcing steps, and discuss automated heuristics to reduce manual work.

concerns.title: Potential preprocessing/delexicalisation artifacts affecting model comparison
concerns.description: Delexicalisation is done via exact token matching; multi-token entities or tokenization mismatches could bias perplexity/BLEU comparisons between datasets.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes 'exact match between entities and tokens' for delexicalisation
Shared analysis flagged delexicalisation assumption (A4) as risky
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide preprocessing details: tokenization rules, how multi-token entities handled, counts of delexicalised tokens, and run sensitivity checks (alternative delexicalisation heuristics) to ensure results are robust.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary comparison dataset (crowdsourced dialog-act-based multi-domain corpus)
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in being crowdsourced, but constructed from small hand-written ontologies with shallow input shapes (depth 1) and higher input repetition; DBPNLG differs by being KB-grounded with deeper input shapes and more attribute diversity.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Sections 2 and 4; references to Wen et al. (2016)

comparable_works.relevance: Prior method for building RDF content and category graphs used by paper
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Methods reused (category graphs, traversal). The current paper extends this with ILP-based selection and staged crowdsourcing.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2: 'follow the procedure outlined in (Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2016)'

comparable_works.relevance: Another automatic KB-text dataset creation approach used as a counterexample
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Lebret et al. created large-scale automatically aligned data but authors argue it lacks adequate semantic match; DBPNLG trades scale for semantic fidelity via crowdsourcing.
comparable_works.source_trace: Introduction note and references

comparable_works.citation_label: Konstas & Lapata, 2013 / Androutsopoulos et al., NaturalOWL
comparable_works.relevance: Works on concept-to-text and ontology verbalisation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Prior art in ontology verbalisers and trainable NLG; the paper positions DBPNLG as resource for KB verbaliser learning with different creation strategy (ILP selection + crowdsourcing).
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature (top_documents) and manuscript references

uncertainty_flags: Missing formal ILP specification, solver choices and runtime; selection sensitivity to bigram model parameters is unknown.
Crowdsourcing verification lacks inter-annotator agreement and per-category error breakdown; 8.7% loss is reported but remaining noise unknown.
Neural evaluation uses a single architecture and fixed 13K balanced sample; results may not generalize to other models, full-dataset sizes, or tuned implementations.
Some comparative metrics/tables referenced (Tables 1–5) are not fully reproduced in the available excerpts; need to confirm whether statistics computed on full datasets or sampled subsets.
Generalisability to other KBs is claimed but empirically demonstrated only on DBpedia categories; scaling cost for property clarification per KB not quantified.
alternative_interpretations: Higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG may reflect increased lexical/vocabulary heterogeneity (domain names, rare entities) or delexicalisation artifacts rather than structural micro-planning difficulty per se.

The ILP objective maximizing bigram probability could bias toward frequently co-occurring but stereotyped property subsets, producing some forms of statistical regularity that interact unintentionally with model learning (either making some patterns easier or harder).

Crowd merging of single-triple verbalizations may limit natural discourse-level strategies (authors reuse single-triple sentences and instruct workers to merge) so some forms of natural aggregation may be underrepresented relative to fully free-written texts.

The relatively small overall corpus size compared to RNNLG might amplify variance in metrics like CTTR and LS; reported differences may diminish if RNNLG were subsampled differently or DBPNLG scaled up.
transparency_notes: Request authors to release ILP code, SRILM commands and parameters, ILP solver config, and sample category graphs to enable reproduction.
Request anonymized verification logs (crowd judgments per criterion per verbalisation), worker qualification criteria, and counts of banned workers.
Request full numeric tables (Tables 1–5) and the code used for metric computation (tokenization, POS tagging, CTTR/LS scripts) to reproduce textual analyses.
Authors should provide the exact preprocessing and delexicalisation scripts (tokenization, entity-to-slot mapping) used in neural experiments.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The pipeline's combination of ILP-guided subtree extraction from large KB category graphs and staged single-triple crowdsourced verbalisation/merging appears not to have close direct analogs among standard crowdsourced NLG corpora—which supports a novelty signal—however novelty does not substitute for empirical validation of claims (reproducibility, annotation reliability, and model-based evidence that micro-planning is learned).
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ILP formulation and solver are published and show stable selection across parameter settings and categories, the method can be reliably reproduced.
If verification logs show high inter-annotator agreement and low residual semantic errors, the corpus can indeed focus evaluations on micro-planning.

If broader modeling experiments (multiple architectures, larger sample sizes) consistently show DBPNLG induces higher difficulty for operations like aggregation/referring generation, the resource will be validated as more challenging.
If automated or semi-automated property clarification methods reduce manual effort, the pipeline can scale to many KBs without prohibitive human cost.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines known components (KB graph extraction, co-occurrence models, ILP selection, crowdsourcing) into a focused pipeline aimed at micro-planning; the idea is an incremental synthesis rather than a disruptive paradigm shift.
evidence: References to Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016) and Wen et al. (2016) show components are drawn from prior work
Manuscript emphasizes new combination and explicit focus on input-shape-driven linguistic diversity
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty depends on ILP selection specifics and originality of the merging/validation procedure; those details are partially absent.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Potentially disruptive in practice if scaled and validated
novelty_lenses.rationale: If the pipeline reliably produces KB-grounded, diverse corpora with high semantic fidelity and if it generalises across KBs, it would materially shift corpus creation strategies toward KB-driven benchmarking for micro-planning tasks.
evidence: DBPNLG statistics showing deeper shapes and richer lexical/syntactic metrics compared to RNNLG
Claims of applicability to other RDF KBs and plan to release as a shared task resource
uncertainty_flags: Scaling and reproducibility gaps (ILP and crowdsourcing details) and lack of multi-KB demonstrations temper the disruptive interpretation.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects high certainty in the paper's descriptions (pipeline, reported statistics, crowdsourcing steps) but moderate-to-high uncertainty about methodological sufficiency for some claims (generalisation, model-difficulty as an intrinsic property, and verification reliability). Lower bound acknowledges possible issues if missing details materially change outcomes; upper bound reflects the strong descriptive evidence and multiple corroborating analyses in the manuscript.

consensus_findings: The manuscript presents a coherent, modular semi-automatic pipeline (category-graph extraction + SRILM bigram models + ILP subtree selection + staged crowdsourcing with validators and majority-vote verification) for creating a KB-grounded data-to-text corpus (DBPNLG).

DBPNLG is empirically described as having greater structural and lexical diversity than the RNNLG benchmark by multiple metrics reported in the paper (more attributes, many more input shapes including deeper trees, longer/more multi-sentence texts, higher CTTR and lexical sophistication).

Crowdsourcing included several practical quality-control mechanisms (manual property clarification, JS validators, spot checks, five-way verification) and an aggregate post-verification corpus loss of 8.7% is reported.

The authors ran a baseline neural generation comparison (a 3-layer seq2seq with attention trained on balanced 13K samples per dataset) and report higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG, suggesting increased challenge for at least that baseline and preprocessing pipeline.

Important details required for reproducibility and stronger interpretation are missing or under-specified in the manuscript (formal ILP specification and solver settings; per-criterion inter-annotator agreement and validation logs; full numeric tables and sampling details; delexicalisation/tokenization scripts).
disagreements: How strongly the neural experiments support the claim that DBPNLG is intrinsically 'harder' for generation: some reviewers treat the single-baseline result as meaningful evidence of increased challenge; others view it as suggestive but insufficient without multiple architectures, hyperparameter tuning, variance reporting and training-size scaling studies.

Degree of methodological novelty: some reviewers view the integration of ILP-driven KB selection with staged crowdsourcing as a useful incremental engineering novelty; others consider the combination potentially novel and practically impactful but emphasize that novelty depends on omitted ILP details and validation.

Extent to which bigram co-occurrence (sibling/chain models) is a valid proxy for human judgments of coherence: reviewers differ on whether the presented motivation is sufficient (some see it as plausible and pragmatic) versus requiring human-rated intrinsic validation to claim content-selection quality.

Generalisability to other RDF KBs: some reviewers accept the claim as plausible (pipeline components are general), while others require empirical runs or quantified manual effort estimates to accept cross-KB scalability.
uncertainty_hotspots: ILP content-selection: absence of the formal ILP objective, constraints, solver identity and parameters (tie-breaking, regularization, runtime) makes it unclear whether selection biases or implementation choices drive reported shape diversity.

Intrinsic coherence validation: no human-rating study reported comparing ILP-selected subgraphs to baselines (random, frequency-based, greedy), so alignment between bigram scores and human coherence is untested.

Crowd verification reliability: missing inter-annotator agreement (kappa/IAA) per criterion, per-category rejection breakdowns, and anonymized verification logs leave the residual semantic-noise rate unknown beyond the aggregate 8.7% loss.

Neural evaluation generality: results rest on a single seq2seq implementation, one training-size sampling strategy (balanced 13K), single delexicalisation method (exact-token matching), and no variance/statistical-significance reporting. This limits claims that DBPNLG is broadly harder for modern generation systems.

Preprocessing / delexicalisation artifacts: exact-token matching may miss multi-token entities or morphological variants. The impact of tokenization and delexicalisation choices on perplexity/BLEU comparisons is not ablated.
Scaling and manual effort: manual property clarification per category is reported but not quantified across categories or KBs; the time/effort cost and automation potential are uncertain.

Metric provenance and subsets: some comparative metrics and tables are referenced but not shown in full in the submission excerpt; it is unclear in several cases whether metrics were computed on full datasets or on the sampled balanced subsets used for neural experiments.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-analyst reviewers emphasized logical coherence and the chain of inference (content selection -> shape diversity -> syntactic phenomena -> learning difficulty), highlighting missing formal links (ILP math, solver details) and the need for ablations linking selection choices to dataset statistics.

Methodology-auditor reviewers prioritized reproducibility and validity: they flagged missing artifacts (code, SRILM commands, validator scripts, annotation logs), requested inter-annotator agreement measures, and proposed concrete robustness experiments (alternative selection baselines, human coherence ratings).

Novelty-assessor reviewers (incremental and disruptive lenses) focused on how novel the integration is relative to prior art and whether the resource delivers community value; their assessments depend heavily on whether the omitted methodological details and validation experiments are provided.

Claim-verifier reviewers prioritized direct evidence for each asserted claim and highlighted where evidence was indirect (e.g., micro-planning suitability inferred from corpus phenomena rather than demonstrated via targeted probes).

These role-conditioned emphases produced complementary but sometimes divergent priorities: some reviewers recommended more intrinsic evaluations (human judgments of coherence), others more external validations (multiple model families and training scales), and others focused on artifact release for reproducibility.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Maintain the editorial role as arbiter of completeness and reproducibility. Request the authors to address the key methodological and transparency gaps before further consideration. Specifically, ask for (1) a formal specification of the ILP (objective, variables, constraints), solver name/version and typical runtimes; (2) SRILM training commands, smoothing/interpolation details and corpus samples used to learn bigrams; (3) full crowdsourcing verification statistics including per-criterion inter-annotator agreement, per-category rejection rates, anonymized verification logs or aggregated vote distributions, and counts of banned workers; (4) all full numeric tables referenced (per-category counts, shapes, attribute inventories) and clarification whether results are on full datasets or balanced/sampled subsets; (5) code/scripts for preprocessing and delexicalisation and a report on how multi-token entities were handled (plus ablation showing sensitivity of neural results to delex choices); (6) expanded neural experiments that at minimum include (a) one additional tuned/representative architecture (e.g., the community implementation used by Wen et al. or a transformer-based model), (b) multiple runs to report variance, and (c) learning curves across training sizes; (7) an intrinsic human evaluation of ILP-selected subgraphs vs reasonable baselines (random/frequency/greedy) to validate the bigram/ILP coherence proxy; and (8) a concise per-category summary of manual property-clarification effort to substantiate generalisability claims. Where authors cannot provide new experiments within revision constraints, require clear statements of limitations and plans/datasets/code to be released on publication for reproducibility. Keep decision-making centrally in the editor's purview using these evidence items to judge sufficiency for publication.
meta_review.author_guidance: Provide concrete reproducibility artifacts and targeted validation experiments to strengthen and clarify claims. Prioritize: (A) Release the ILP mathematical formulation, solver invocation and parameters, representative ILP instances and runtimes, and add an ablation showing how shape diversity and selected-property distributions change with S/C/M model variants and with random or frequency-based baselines. (B) Publish SRILM training commands, smoothing/interpolation weights and the corpora used to compute bigrams. (C) Provide anonymized verification logs or aggregated vote distributions, compute inter-annotator agreement (per criterion), report per-category rejection rates, and show representative examples of rejected and borderline verbalizations. (D) Expand neural evaluation: run at least one additional tuned model (or the optimized codebase used in related work), report multiple runs with seed variance and statistical tests, and show learning curves for varying training-set sizes; include an ablation for delexicalisation/tokenization choices and report how many entity mentions failed exact matching. (E) Run an intrinsic human coherence study comparing ILP-selected subgraphs to plausible baselines and report correlation with bigram scores. (F) Quantify manual property-clarification effort per category (number of properties clarified, person-hours) and, if possible, include a small proof-of-concept application on another KB or on additional DBpedia categories to support generalisability. (G) Release code and data (ILP code, bigram scripts, validator scripts, preprocessing, dataset splits) or clearly document why some items cannot be shared. In the revised manuscript, explicitly state remaining limitations and how they affect the scope of claims (e.g., that model-difficulty claims are currently limited to the evaluated baseline and preprocessing choices).

Missing or requested artifact: SRILM training scripts/commands, vocabulary and smoothing/interpolation settings, corpora samples used to learn sibling/chain/interpolated bigram models.
Missing or requested artifact: full numeric tables (all referenced Tables 1–5) with per-category breakdowns and explicit statement which analyses use full datasets versus balanced/sampled subsets.
Missing or requested artifact: preprocessing and delexicalisation scripts (tokenization rules, entity-to-slot mapping), counts of delexicalised instances, and handling rules for multi-token entities.

Missing or requested artifact: anonymized crowdsourcing verification logs or aggregated vote distributions, per-criterion inter-annotator agreement measures (e.g., Fleiss' kappa), per-category rejection rates, examples of removed vs accepted pairs, and worker filtering statistics.

epistemic_limits: Causal inference limit: The presented evidence links dataset structural properties to increased difficulty for one seq2seq baseline, but this does not establish a causal generalization to all generation models or settings—different architectures or preprocessing can alter observed difficulty.

Validation limit: Without inter-annotator agreement and error-type breakdowns, the aggregate 8.7% removal rate does not fully characterize residual semantic mismatches or per-category variability; thus claims that the dataset cleanly isolates micro-planning from content-selection errors are provisional.

Selection-proxy limit: Using bigram sibling/chain co-occurrence as a proxy for human judgments of coherence is plausible but not empirically validated in the manuscript; conclusions depending on content-selection quality require human-in-the-loop validation.

Reproducibility limit: Missing ILP, SRILM and preprocessing artifacts impede exact reproduction; some observed dataset statistics and downstream results could be sensitive to implementation choices not currently disclosed.

Generalisability limit: Empirical evidence is limited to six DBpedia categories (authors mention more collected categories without detailed reporting); scaling behavior and manual clarifications required for other KBs remain uncertain.

Measurement limit: Some metrics (e.g., CTTR, lexical sophistication, vocabulary size) are sensitive to tokenization and delexicalisation; without detailed preprocessing descriptions, comparisons across datasets may partly reflect pipeline differences rather than solely dataset-intrinsic properties.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes a semi-automatic pipeline that extracts category graphs from DBpedia, learns sibling/chain/interpolated property bigram models (SRILM), uses an ILP to select subtrees (1–7 triples) as input shapes, and collects/validates human verbalizations via a four-step CrowdFlower workflow to produce DBPNLG. The paper compares DBPNLG to the RNNLG benchmark across data-structure metrics (attributes, input-patterns, shapes), textual complexity measures (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), and baseline generation difficulty (one 3-layer seq2seq with attention on balanced 13K samples). The authors report DBPNLG has more diverse/deeper input shapes, lexically and syntactically richer texts, a low post-verification discard rate (~8.7%), and that the examined seq2seq baseline performs worse on DBPNLG (higher perplexity, lower BLEU).
strengths: Clear, modular pipeline combining KB-driven content selection (category graphs + bigram models + ILP) with a staged crowdsourcing protocol (clarify properties; single-triple verbalizations; merge; five-way verification).

Multi-dimensional empirical comparison against an established crowdsourced benchmark (RNNLG) using interpretable metrics linking input-structure diversity to textual variety (attributes, shapes, inputs-per-pattern, CTTR, lexical sophistication, texts-per-input).

Practical quality-control in crowdsourcing: property clarification, automated validators, manual checks, and multi-annotator verification with an explicit rejection rule and reported aggregate corpus loss.
limitations: ILP content-selection under-specified: the manuscript omits the formal ILP objective, variables/constraints, solver identity and parameters, runtimes, and sensitivity analyses — this impedes reproducibility and raises the possibility that implementation choices (not the conceptual approach) drive reported shape diversity.

Crowd verification reporting incomplete: only an aggregate 8.7% corpus loss is given; there are no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Fleiss' kappa), per-criterion or per-category rejection breakdowns, or representative examples of removed vs retained borderline cases, leaving residual semantic-noise rates unclear.

Neural evaluation narrow in scope: model-difficulty claims rest on a single seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow tutorial), one balanced training size (13K), a single delexicalisation strategy (exact-token matching), and no variance/statistical-significance reporting — limiting generality of the claim that DBPNLG is intrinsically harder.

Intrinsic coherence proxy unvalidated: bigram sibling/chain co-occurrence is assumed to proxy human judgments of coherence for subgraph selection, but no human study compares ILP-selected subgraphs to reasonable baselines (random, frequency-based, greedy), so selection quality is not empirically established.
open_questions: Please provide the formal ILP mathematical formulation (objective, decision variables, constraints), the solver name/version and invocation parameters, typical runtimes per instance, and a short ablation showing how shape diversity and selected-property distributions change with S-Model vs C-Model vs M-Model and versus simple baselines.

Provide verification reliability metrics: per-criterion inter-annotator agreement, per-category verification/rejection rates, aggregated vote distributions or anonymized verification logs, and examples of rejected and borderline verbalizations to characterize residual semantic errors.

Extend or clarify neural evaluation: how sensitive are perplexity/BLEU differences to delexicalisation choices (how many multi-token entities failed exact matching), to random seeds, and to alternative architectures/hyperparameters (e.g., Wen et al.'s implementation, pointer/copy or transformer variants)? Provide variance across runs and statistical tests or learning curves across training sizes.

If claiming generalisability to other RDF KBs, quantify the manual property-clarification effort per category (number of properties clarified; person-hours) and, if available, report at least a small application on an additional KB or additional DBpedia categories to show scalability.

How were bigram models trained exactly (SRILM commands, smoothing/interpolation parameters, corpora used, vocabulary cutoffs)? Please make those scripts/configs available to reproduce property co-occurrence estimates.

Do the authors have a diagnostic or targeted evaluation (or plans) to directly test micro-planning subtasks (aggregation, referring expression generation, sentence segmentation) rather than inferring suitability from corpus phenomena? If absent, can they supply a prioritized plan or initial probes?
consensus_snapshot: The pipeline and resource (DBPNLG) are coherently described and aimed at producing KB-grounded inputs with greater structural and lexical diversity than RNNLG.

Multiple descriptive metrics in the manuscript indicate DBPNLG contains more attributes, many more input shapes (including deeper trees), longer/more multi-sentence texts, and higher lexical diversity measures.
Authors implemented practical crowdsourcing safeguards and report a modest post-verification discard rate (~8.7%).
The single examined seq2seq baseline shows higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG under the described preprocessing, suggesting increased difficulty for at least that configuration.
disagreement_snapshot: Strength of evidence that DBPNLG is broadly and intrinsically 'harder' for modern generation systems: some reviewers see the single-baseline result as meaningful evidence of increased challenge; others regard it as suggestive but insufficient without broader model families, tuning, variance estimates, and delexicalisation ablations.

Adequacy of bigram-based ILP selection as a human-relevant coherence model: some find the approach plausible/pragmatic, while others require human-rated intrinsic validation before accepting content-selection quality claims.

Degree of novelty: reviewers differ between seeing the contribution as a useful engineering synthesis of known components versus a practically novel pipeline whose value depends on omitted implementation/validation details.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about whether reported diversity metrics and model-difficulty effects hold when ILP, SRILM, and preprocessing are fully disclosed and when alternative selection baselines or model architectures are tested.
Uncertainty about the residual level and types of semantic mismatches after verification due to missing IAA and verification logs.
Uncertainty about scalability/generalizability to other KBs because per-category manual clarification effort and multi-KB trials are not reported.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper introduces DBPNLG, built by extracting KB category graphs, learning property bigrams (SRILM), selecting subtrees via ILP (1–7 triples) to induce varied input shapes, and collecting/verifying human texts through a staged CrowdFlower pipeline. Comparative analyses versus RNNLG show DBPNLG has more attributes, many more input shapes (including deeper trees), longer and lexically richer texts, and fewer repeated inputs-per-pattern. The authors report a modest 8.7% corpus loss after verification and find a single seq2seq baseline attains higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG under the described preprocessing, suggesting increased modeling challenge.
Strengths: The pipeline is explicit and modular, the empirical analysis is multi-faceted and interpretable, and the crowdsourcing workflow incorporates several reasonable quality-control mechanisms. The focus on input-shape-driven linguistic diversity is a clear and useful design principle for micro-planning research.
Limitations: (1) Key reproducibility details are missing (formal ILP, solver/config, SRILM commands, preprocessing/delex scripts), preventing exact replication and leaving open whether results are sensitive to implementation choices. (2) Crowdsourcing verification lacks inter-annotator agreement and per-category error analyses, so residual semantic-noise rates and validator effectiveness are uncertain. (3) Neural evaluation uses only one seq2seq baseline, one training-size sampling strategy, and a single delexicalisation method without variance/statistical testing; thus claims about intrinsic dataset difficulty need broader empirical support. (4) The use of bigram co-occurrence as a coherence proxy is not backed by an intrinsic human validation study.
Open Questions: See above list (six reviewer-style requests for ILP formalization, verification metrics, neural sensitivity experiments, generalisability effort quantification, SRILM details, targeted micro-planning probes).
Transparency: Requested artifacts include ILP code/formulation and solver configs, SRILM training scripts and bigram models, full numeric tables and dataset splits, preprocessing and delexicalisation scripts, crowdsourcing verification logs or aggregated vote distributions with IAA, and neural experiment code/configs with seeds and training curves. Releasing the DBPNLG dataset with selection metadata (which selection model produced each input) would materially aid reuse and validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence in the descriptive claims about the pipeline and reported dataset statistics is moderate-to-high given within-manuscript consistency across multiple metrics and procedural detail. Confidence is lower regarding broader inferences (intrinsic dataset difficulty across architectures, content-selection alignment with human judgments, and cross-KB generalisability) because key reproducibility artifacts, agreement statistics and robustness experiments are missing. The interval reflects strong support for the resource's described construction but notable epistemic uncertainty around several inferential leaps.
